Saturday, 25 October 2036, Goethe-Institut Berlin. Elena is in the oral exam, part two. Her partner is Yusuf, a young engineer from Aleppo. Topic: “Sollen Städte Autos aus dem Zentrum verbannen?” (Should cities ban cars from the centre?)
I think cars should be banned from the centre completely. The air would be better, and the streets would belong to people again.
That's an interesting point and I partly agree with you. However, I'm thinking of elderly people. My daughter-in-law's grandfather is eighty-eight. He can't walk far.
But it's precisely for him that there would then be more trams and buses. How does he get into town now?
By tram, that's true. He actually used to be a tram driver. But not everyone lives near a line. What do you think of an exception for people with disabilities and for deliveries?
I would agree with that. In Aleppo there used to be an old town without cars. The merchants brought their goods with donkeys. Maybe not with donkeys, but with small electric vehicles?
I like that. In Sibiu too, where I come from, the old town is almost car-free, and the shops still thrive. So could we say: cars out, but with smart exceptions?
Exactly. A centre for people, but nobody must be excluded. We can agree on that.
Agreed. And we'll keep your donkeys as plan B.
1. Structure of the Sprechen module (Goethe B2)
you choose one of two topics and make notes
you speak alone about the chosen topic, then answer a question from your partner / the examiner
you discuss a controversial topic with your partner, you both argue and reach a conclusion
The exam is usually taken in pairs. The exact details may vary; check the official Modellsatz and look on the Goethe-Institut website for a video of a model oral exam.

What counts is engaging in dialogue (auf den Partner eingehen): pick up what your partner said (“Sie haben gesagt, dass … Das finde ich …”), don't just give monologues.

On Saturday, the twenty-fifth of October two thousand and thirty-six, Elena woke up at five in the morning, although the exam didn't start until nine, and went to the kitchen on the first floor, where, to her surprise, the light was already on. Lena was there, of course, because she got up every morning at four, and instead of going to the bakery she had made breakfast. On the table there were fresh rolls, a jar of Dan's acacia honey, a teapot and, in the middle, a small cake in the shape of a book, with an inscription in icing: “B2”. Next to it was a note from Elif, who at that hour was of course still asleep, with the card from the listening training and a new line underneath, in red writing: “5. If you're nervous: think of the cake.”

At six Elena's phone rang. It was Mrs Petersen from the care home, who was on a very early shift and who, as she put it, had a message to pass on. Grete had been awake for a little while during the night, had asked the date, and when she was told it was the twenty-fifth of October, she had said: “The Romanian woman has her exam today. Tell her something from me.” And then, after a long pause, so quietly that Mrs Petersen had to lean down: “Not every note. The melody.” Mrs Petersen didn't know what it meant and apologised for that. Elena knew. She said thank you, hung up and sat motionless for a while at the kitchen table, her cup of tea in both hands. Then she wrote the words on the back of Elif's note, under the fifth point, as the sixth: “Not every note. The melody. G.”

At half past seven Andrei took her to the stop. He had offered to drive her, but Elena had refused. She wanted to go by tram. On the M1, to the Rosenthaler Platz stop, from there on foot to Neue Schönhauser Straße. And when the tram came, she saw in the cab a young man in a BVG uniform, with a man with a moustache beside him, and the young man rang the bell when he saw her. Twice. Elena laughed. Leo, as she found out later, had swapped shifts with a colleague so as to drive exactly this tram, at exactly this time. Mr Schäfer, who was standing beside him, hadn't minded. He had only said: “Twice is actually for sad occasions.” And Leo had replied: “At Hotte's. With us, twice is for exams.”

First came the written parts: reading, listening, writing, in a large, bright room on the third floor of the Goethe-Institut, with twenty other candidates from fourteen countries. Elena read the tasks first. She didn't read every word. She listened for the melody. She stopped at every stop, all four points in the forum post, all three in the email. She wrote “Mit freundlichen Grüßen” and checked it three times. And when she came out of the room at half past twelve for the lunch break, she was as tired as she had last been after a night at the apiary, when Dan had caught a swarm. She sat down on a bench in the institute's courtyard, ate the last piece of Lena's book cake and thought about nothing.

She did think about one moment, though, later, on the way home. In the reading test, in part two, in an article about the disappearance of bees in Europe, which seemed to her as if Dan had ordered it, there was a sentence: “For agriculture, bees are indispensable.” Elena had seen the word, and for a moment she was no longer in the exam room but in the cellar at number thirty-three, with Elif writing “un-, verzichten, -bar” in the margin, and with the smell of Lena's cake from the café. “Like honey”, she had thought, and had almost laughed out loud, and the examiner walking between the tables had given her a brief, stern look. Elena had answered the question correctly. Of that she was sure. It was the only question she was completely sure about.

The oral exam was at two p.m. Elena had fifteen minutes of preparation, in a small room with a table and a clock on the wall. She could choose between two topics: “Volunteering — should it become compulsory?” and “Lifelong learning”. She chose the second, without hesitating. She wrote five keyword lines on a sheet: “Me — 5 years — the kitchen table — Sibiu.” “Advantages: brain, contacts, family.” “Disadvantages: time, money, fear.” “Example: Grete, 100, still learning.” “Conclusion: you're never too old, but never alone.” Then she looked at the clock, closed her eyes and thought of Ludwig, who had told her the evening before: “Talk the way you talk to me. Not the way you talk to an examiner. And the examiner is just a person who wants the hour to pass quickly.”

In the exam room sat two examiners, one older, with grey curls, and one younger, with glasses, and next to Elena, on the second chair, her exam partner: a young man of about thirty, thin, with a friendly, nervous smile, who introduced himself as Yusuf, civil engineer, from Aleppo, four years in Berlin. He was holding a pen so tightly that his knuckles had gone white. Elena saw it and thought of Leo in March, of the hand that couldn't let go of the control lever. She leaned towards Yusuf before the examiner began and whispered in German: “Breathe. And think of the cake.” Yusuf looked at her, puzzled. Then he laughed, quietly, and his hand relaxed.

Elena gave her presentation. She didn't look at her sheet, or only twice, briefly, the way Leo looked at his screen. She talked about the five years at the kitchen table in Sibiu, in the evenings, after work, with nobody to correct her. She talked about the advantages of learning in old age, about the brain, which is like a muscle, and about the contacts you find, “sometimes people you would never have met, a twelve-year-old girl for example, who teaches you how to read”. She talked about the disadvantages, honestly, about the fear of making a fool of yourself, which doesn't decrease with age but grows. And then she talked about Grete. About a woman who at a hundred still listened every Wednesday to a child playing the piano and who, as she put it, “is still learning something new, namely how to let go”.

The room was quiet when Elena finished. The older examiner noted something down and then looked up. She asked a question, as the exam required: “You said that fear grows with age. What would you recommend to someone who wants to start learning a language at sixty but is afraid?” Elena thought for a moment. Then she said: “I'd recommend they find a teacher younger than their grandchildren. Children aren't afraid of mistakes. It's contagious.” The younger examiner laughed, the older one smiled, and Yusuf, who was sitting beside her, nodded so hard that Elena thought his head would fall off.

Then came Yusuf's presentation, on volunteering, and he gave it well, even if too fast at the start, and Elena asked him the question she was supposed to ask, and then came part two, the discussion. The topic was on a sheet that the younger examiner placed between them: “Should cities drive cars out of the centre?” Yusuf was for it, firmly. Elena was unsure. And so it became a real discussion, not a rehearsed one, with arguments that came not from a textbook but from two lives. Yusuf told them about the old town of Aleppo, as it had been before the war, with its narrow car-free lanes, with merchants and donkeys and the smell of soap and spices. Elena told them about Ludwig, eighty-eight, who couldn't walk far any more, and about the old centre of Sibiu, which was also almost car-free. And at some point, without having planned it, they found a compromise, and it was a better compromise than any in Elena's notebook.

When they came out of the exam room, Yusuf stood with Elena in the corridor for a while, and neither knew what to say. Then Yusuf said, in German, quietly: “My mother stayed in Aleppo too. She's sixty. She wants to learn German so she can visit me. She's afraid.” He hesitated. “I'll tell her to find a teacher younger than her grandchildren.” Elena took her twelfth notebook out of her bag, tore out the page with Elif's card, the five points, and gave it to him. “For your mother”, she said. “With cake.” Yusuf took the page, folded it carefully and put it in his wallet, next to a photo of a woman in a white headscarf standing in front of an old house with a green door.

Outside, in front of the Goethe-Institut, they were waiting. Andrei and Lena. Elif with her mother. Ludwig, with his walking stick, in his tram driver's cap, who had insisted on coming by tram, in Leo's tram, of course, in the seat just behind the cab. And Hotte, with two walking sticks and a little bunch of supermarket flowers, which, as he explained at once, he had bought “just by chance”, because he happened to be in the area anyway. Elena came down the steps, slowly, and stopped on the last step. She didn't know the result yet. She would only find out in a few weeks. But she saw the faces and said, in German, loudly enough for everyone to hear: “I didn't understand every word. But I understood everything.”

On the way home, on the M1, Elena sat next to Ludwig, in the seat behind the cab, and Leo drove the way you carry a cup of coffee. Ludwig didn't ask about the exam. He only asked: “And Yusuf? Was he good?” Elena nodded. “Better than me”, she said. “He offered the donkeys as plan B.” Ludwig laughed. Then he fell silent and looked out of the window, at Kastanienallee passing by, with its yellow leaves and the lights just coming on. “You know”, he said after a while, “when I was Yusuf's age, I'd never have believed that one day I'd be sitting in a tram with a Romanian woman who had just taken a German exam, and that my grandson would be driving.” He fell silent. “Ingrid would have believed it”, he added. “She always believed everything. I just followed her.”

In the evening, after dinner in the café, when the glasses were empty and Hotte had told for the third time how he had bought the flowers “purely by chance”, Elena called Dan, on video, and Dan was sitting in the kitchen in Sibiu, with the old German exercise book from nineteen eighty-eight in front of him, which he had kept next to the phone for weeks. “Ei?” (“Well?”), he asked in Romanian. Elena answered in German. “I don't know yet”, she said. “But I've written page five.” Then she took a pen and a sheet of paper, wrote something on it and held it up to the camera. Dan put on his glasses. He read slowly, word by word, moving his lips, the way he had read forty-eight years before. On the sheet it said: “Ich heiße Elena. Ich bin die Frau des Imkers. Ich spreche Deutsch.” Dan said nothing for a long time. Then he stuck the sheet, which he had printed out when Elena sent it to him, onto page five of his old exercise book.
